title: Algorithms and data structures
summary: Searching, sorting, stacks, trees, heaps, graphs, dynamic programming and backtracking, one idea per lesson, each with a Lab that traces it step by step.

lessons.title: Halve a sorted list with binary search
lessons.body:
# Halve a sorted list with binary search

A sorted list lets you discard half of the remaining items with one comparison. Keep two bounds, lo and hi, around the part that can still contain the target. Look at the middle, then move one bound past it.

```python
items = [2, 5, 8, 13, 21]
lo, hi = 0, len(items) - 1
mid = (lo + hi) // 2   # 2 -> items[2] is 8
```

## Think before coding

Each step removes at least the middle item, so the loop ends after about log2(n) steps. Use lo <= hi with inclusive bounds and move to mid + 1 or mid - 1, never to mid itself, or a two-item range can loop forever. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write binary_search(items, target) for a sorted list. Return an index where items holds target, or -1 when it is absent.

checks.name: large list
checks.code: big = list(range(0, 2_000_000, 2)); assert binary_search(big, 1_999_998) == 999_999 and binary_search(big, 7) == -1

hints: Start with lo = 0 and hi = len(items) - 1.
Compare items[mid] with target to decide which half survives.
Move lo to mid + 1 or hi to mid - 1 so the range always shrinks.
lessons.explanation: Each step removes at least the middle item, so the loop ends after about log2(n) steps. Use lo <= hi with inclusive bounds and move to mid + 1 or mid - 1, never to mid itself, or a two-item range can loop forever.

lessons.title: Meet in the middle with two pointers
lessons.body:
# Meet in the middle with two pointers

In a sorted list, a pair that sums too low needs a larger left value and a pair that sums too high needs a smaller right value. Two indices moving toward each other test every useful pair once.

```python
items = [1, 3, 4, 6, 9]
left, right = 0, len(items) - 1
print(items[left] + items[right])   # 10
```

## Think before coding

When the sum is too small, no pair using the current left value can work with any smaller right value, so the left value is finished. The symmetric argument retires the right value. The scan is linear instead of quadratic. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write pair_with_sum(items, target) for a sorted list. Return a tuple of two indices (i, j) with i < j whose values add up to target, or None.

checks.name: one value cannot pair with itself
checks.code: assert pair_with_sum([5], 10) is None and pair_with_sum([], 0) is None

hints: Start with one index at each end.
Compare the sum with target.
Move left up when the sum is small, right down when it is large.
lessons.explanation: When the sum is too small, no pair using the current left value can work with any smaller right value, so the left value is finished. The symmetric argument retires the right value. The scan is linear instead of quadratic.

lessons.title: Slide a window over the longest unique run
lessons.body:
# Slide a window over the longest unique run

A window is a slice described by two indices. Grow it on the right one character at a time. When the new character is already inside, move the left edge just past its previous position instead of starting over.

```python
last = {}
text = "abcab"
# at index 3, 'a' was seen at 0
# so left moves to 1
```

## Think before coding

Remember where each character was last seen. The left edge only moves forward, so each index enters and leaves the window once and the whole scan is linear. Take the maximum width after each step. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write longest_unique(text) returning the length of the longest substring with no repeated character.
hints: Keep a dictionary from character to its last index.
Move left only when the repeat is inside the window.
Update the best width after storing the new index.
lessons.explanation: Remember where each character was last seen. The left edge only moves forward, so each index enters and leaves the window once and the whole scan is linear. Take the maximum width after each step.

lessons.title: Merge overlapping intervals after sorting
lessons.body:
# Merge overlapping intervals after sorting

Overlapping meetings, ranges of free memory and booked dates all reduce to intervals. Sorting by start puts every overlap next to each other, so one pass can merge them.

```python
spans = sorted([(5, 8), (1, 3), (2, 4)])
print(spans)   # [(1, 3), (2, 4), (5, 8)]
```

## Think before coding

After sorting, an interval either starts inside the last merged one, which extends its end, or starts after it, which closes it and opens a new one. Use max for the end, because a short interval can sit entirely inside a longer one. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write merge(intervals) taking (start, end) tuples. Return the merged, sorted list; touching intervals such as (1, 2) and (2, 3) merge too. Leave the input list unchanged.
hints: Sort a copy by start.
Compare each start with the end of the last merged interval.
Extend with max(end) or append a new interval.
lessons.explanation: After sorting, an interval either starts inside the last merged one, which extends its end, or starts after it, which closes it and opens a new one. Use max for the end, because a short interval can sit entirely inside a longer one.

lessons.title: Match brackets with a stack
lessons.body:
# Match brackets with a stack

The most recently opened bracket must close first. That last-in, first-out order is exactly what a stack gives you: push every opener, and every closer must match the top.

```python
stack = []
for char in "([])":
    print(char, stack)
```

## Think before coding

A closer is wrong when the stack is empty or its top is a different kind. At the end, anything still on the stack was never closed. Other characters are ignored, so the same check works on code or formulas. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write balanced(text) returning True when every (, [ and { is closed by its own kind in the right order. Ignore all other characters.

checks.name: unclosed and extra closer
checks.code: assert not balanced('((') and not balanced('())')

hints: Push each opening bracket.
On a closer, pop and compare with its partner.
The text is balanced only if the stack ends empty.
lessons.explanation: A closer is wrong when the stack is empty or its top is a different kind. At the end, anything still on the stack was never closed. Other characters are ignored, so the same check works on code or formulas.

lessons.title: Rotate a queue to eliminate players
lessons.body:
# Rotate a queue to eliminate players

A queue serves items in arrival order. collections.deque removes from the front in constant time, unlike list.pop(0), which shifts every remaining item.

```python
from collections import deque
line = deque(["Ann", "Bob", "Cy"])
line.rotate(-1)
print(line)   # deque(['Bob', 'Cy', 'Ann'])
```

## Think before coding

Passing the item k times is the same as moving k people from the front to the back. The person now at the front is out. Repeat until the queue is empty, recording the order people leave. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write elimination_order(names, k): pass k times around the queue, remove whoever is at the front, and repeat. Return the names in the order they leave. Do not modify names.
lessons.solution:
from collections import deque

def elimination_order(names, k):
    line = deque(names)
    order = []
    while line:
        line.rotate(-k)
        order.append(line.popleft())
    return order

checks.name: input intact
checks.code: n=['x','y']; elimination_order(n, 1); assert n == ['x','y'] and elimination_order([], 3) == []

hints: Copy names into a deque.
rotate(-k) moves k people from front to back.
popleft() removes the player who is out.
lessons.explanation: Passing the item k times is the same as moving k people from the front to the back. The person now at the front is out. Repeat until the queue is empty, recording the order people leave.

lessons.title: Build permutations by fixing one item
lessons.body:
# Build permutations by fixing one item

A recursive function solves a problem by trusting a smaller copy of itself. To order n items, choose which item goes first, then ask for every ordering of the remaining items.

```python
def count(n):
    return 1 if n <= 1 else n * count(n - 1)
print(count(4))   # 24 orderings
```

## Think before coding

The base case is an empty list, which has exactly one ordering: the empty one. Each level loops over the items, removes one and prefixes it to every smaller ordering. Removing by position keeps repeated values correct. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write permutations(items) returning every ordering of items as a list of lists, in the order produced by choosing positions left to right.
hints: Return [[]] for an empty list.
Loop over positions and remove that item.
Prefix it to each permutation of the rest.
lessons.explanation: The base case is an empty list, which has exactly one ordering: the empty one. Each level loops over the items, removes one and prefixes it to every smaller ordering. Removing by position keeps repeated values correct.

lessons.title: List every subset with include or skip
lessons.body:
# List every subset with include or skip

Every item faces one decision: in the subset or out. Two choices for each of n items give `2 ** n` subsets. Recursion makes the decision for the first item and lets a smaller call handle the rest.

```python
items = ["a", "b"]
# skip a: [], [b]   take a: [a], [a, b]
```

## Think before coding

The subsets of the rest appear twice: once unchanged and once with the first item added in front. Keeping the skip branch first gives a predictable order, which helps when you compare results. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write subsets(items) returning all `2 ** n` subsets as lists, skip branch first, preserving item order inside each subset.

checks.name: order inside subsets
checks.code: assert all(s == sorted(s) for s in subsets([1,2,3]))

hints: The empty list has one subset.
Compute the subsets of items[1:] once.
Return those, then the same with items[0] in front.
lessons.explanation: The subsets of the rest appear twice: once unchanged and once with the first item added in front. Keeping the skip branch first gives a predictable order, which helps when you compare results.

lessons.title: Insert each item into a sorted prefix
lessons.body:
# Insert each item into a sorted prefix

Insertion sort keeps the left part of the list sorted. Each new item slides left past larger neighbours until it reaches its place, like sorting a hand of cards.

```python
hand = [3, 7, 9, 4]
# 4 moves past 9 and 7, then stops after 3
```

## Think before coding

It takes about n squared steps in the worst case, yet it is fast on nearly sorted data and stable: equal items keep their order because an item stops at the first neighbour that is not larger. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write insertion_sort(items) returning a new sorted list, without calling sorted or list.sort, and without changing items.

checks.name: stable
checks.code:
pairs=[(1,'b'),(0,'x'),(1,'a')]; import functools
class K:
    def __init__(s,p): s.p=p
    def __gt__(s,o): return s.p[0] > o.p[0]
assert [k.p for k in insertion_sort([K(p) for p in pairs])] == [(0,'x'),(1,'b'),(1,'a')]

hints: Copy the list first.
Hold result[i] aside and shift larger items right.
Drop the held value into the gap.
lessons.explanation: It takes about n squared steps in the worst case, yet it is fast on nearly sorted data and stable: equal items keep their order because an item stops at the first neighbour that is not larger.

lessons.title: Sort by splitting and merging
lessons.body:
# Sort by splitting and merging

Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively and merges the two sorted halves. Merging needs only one pass because the smallest remaining item is always at the front of one half.

```python
left, right = [1, 4], [2, 3]
# take 1, then 2, then 3, then 4
```

## Think before coding

There are about log2(n) levels of splitting and each level merges n items, so the total is n log n. Taking from the left half when values are equal keeps the sort stable. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write merge_sort(items) returning a new sorted list using merge sort, without sorted or list.sort.

checks.name: larger
checks.code: import random; r=random.Random(4); a=[r.randint(-50,50) for _ in range(500)]; assert merge_sort(a) == sorted(a)

hints: Lists of length 0 or 1 are already sorted.
Sort both halves recursively.
Merge by repeatedly taking the smaller front item.
lessons.explanation: There are about log2(n) levels of splitting and each level merges n items, so the total is n log n. Taking from the left half when values are equal keeps the sort stable.

lessons.title: Partition around a pivot for quicksort
lessons.body:
# Partition around a pivot for quicksort

Quicksort picks a pivot, moves smaller items before it and larger items after it, then sorts the two sides. The pivot is already in its final place after partitioning.

```python
items = [7, 2, 9, 4]
pivot = items[-1]                     # 4
less = [x for x in items if x < pivot]
print(less)   # [2]
```

## Think before coding

With a fair pivot, each level halves the work and the total is n log n. Grouping values equal to the pivot separately prevents the slowdown on lists full of duplicates. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write quicksort(items) returning a new sorted list. Partition into less, equal and greater lists around a pivot and recurse on less and greater.

checks.name: random
checks.code: import random; r=random.Random(9); a=[r.random() for _ in range(300)]; assert quicksort(a) == sorted(a)

hints: Pick a pivot from the middle.
Build less, equal and greater lists.
Concatenate the sorted sides around equal.
lessons.explanation: With a fair pivot, each level halves the work and the total is n log n. Grouping values equal to the pivot separately prevents the slowdown on lists full of duplicates.

lessons.title: Reverse a linked list in place
lessons.body:
# Reverse a linked list in place

A singly linked list stores each value with a pointer to the next node. Reversing it means turning every arrow around. Three names track the work: the previous node, the current one and the next one you are about to lose.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value, self.next = value, next
head = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))
```

## Think before coding

Save current.next before overwriting it, point current back at prev, then step both forward. When current becomes None, prev is the new head. No new nodes are created, so memory stays constant. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Node(value, next) is provided. Write reverse(head) that reverses the list in place and returns the new head (None for an empty list).

checks.name: three nodes
empty and single
same nodes reused

hints: Start with prev = None and current = head.
Save current.next before changing it.
Return prev when current runs out.
lessons.explanation: Save current.next before overwriting it, point current back at prev, then step both forward. When current becomes None, prev is the new head. No new nodes are created, so memory stays constant.

lessons.title: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers
lessons.body:
# Find the middle with slow and fast pointers

You do not need the length of a linked list to find its middle. Move one pointer one step and another two steps at a time. When the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is halfway.

```python
# 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5
# slow: 1, 2, 3   fast: 1, 3, 5
```

## Think before coding

The same two-speed idea detects cycles, because a fast pointer inside a loop eventually laps the slow one. For an even number of nodes, this version returns the second of the two middle nodes. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Node(value, next) is provided. Write middle(head) returning the middle node in one pass; for an even length return the second middle. Return None for an empty list.

checks.name: odd
even
short

hints: Start both pointers at head.
Loop while fast and fast.next exist.
Move slow once and fast twice per step.
lessons.explanation: The same two-speed idea detects cycles, because a fast pointer inside a loop eventually laps the slow one. For an even number of nodes, this version returns the second of the two middle nodes.

lessons.title: Trade memory for speed with a dictionary
lessons.body:
# Trade memory for speed with a dictionary

Checking every pair of numbers is quadratic. A dictionary remembers values you have already seen and answers "have I seen x?" in constant time on average, so one pass is enough.

```python
seen = {}
for index, value in enumerate([2, 7, 11]):
    seen[value] = index
print(9 - 7 in seen)   # True
```

## Think before coding

For each value, the partner you need is target minus value. Look it up before storing the current value, so an item is never paired with itself, and duplicates still find each other. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write two_sum(items, target) returning indices (i, j) with i < j and items[i] + items[j] == target, choosing the pair whose j is smallest. Return None when no pair exists. The list is not sorted.

checks.name: unsorted and missing
checks.code: assert two_sum([8,1,5,3], 4) == (1,3) and two_sum([], 1) is None

hints: Map each seen value to its index.
Before storing, look up target - value.
Return the stored index and the current one.
lessons.explanation: For each value, the partner you need is target minus value. Look it up before storing the current value, so an item is never paired with itself, and duplicates still find each other.

lessons.title: Insert into a binary search tree
lessons.body:
# Insert into a binary search tree

In a binary search tree every value in a node's left subtree is smaller and every value in its right subtree is larger. Inserting walks down as a search would and attaches a new node where the search falls off the tree.

```python
# 8 has 3 on the left and 10 on the right
# inserting 6: 6 < 8 go left, 6 > 3 go right
```

## Think before coding

Returning the root from the recursive call lets an empty subtree become a new node without special cases. Ignoring duplicates keeps every value unique. An in-order walk of the result lists the values in sorted order. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: TreeNode(value) is provided. Write insert(root, value) returning the root after inserting value; insert into None to start a tree. Ignore a value that is already present.

checks.name: sorted in order
shape
duplicates ignored

hints: An empty tree becomes TreeNode(value).
Go left for smaller values and right for larger ones.
Assign the recursive result back to root.left or root.right.
lessons.explanation: Returning the root from the recursive call lets an empty subtree become a new node without special cases. Ignoring duplicates keeps every value unique. An in-order walk of the result lists the values in sorted order.

lessons.title: Delete from a binary search tree
lessons.body:
# Delete from a binary search tree

Deleting a leaf or a node with one child is easy: replace it with that child. A node with two children needs a stand-in that keeps the ordering, and the smallest value in its right subtree fits exactly.

```python
# delete 3 from: 3 has children 1 and 6
# successor: smallest in right subtree -> 6
```

## Think before coding

Copy the successor's value into the node, then delete that successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so the second deletion is always one of the easy cases. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: TreeNode(value) is provided. Write delete(root, value) returning the root after removing value. Leave the tree unchanged if value is absent.

checks.name: two children
checks.code:
r=None
for v in [8,3,10,1,6,14,4,7]: r=insert(r,v)
r=delete(r,3)
assert inorder(r) == [1,4,6,7,8,10,14]

checks.name: root and leaf
checks.code:
r=None
for v in [5,2,9]: r=insert(r,v)
r=delete(r,5); r=delete(r,2)
assert inorder(r) == [9]

checks.name: missing and empty
checks.code:
r=insert(None,1)
assert inorder(delete(r,42)) == [1] and delete(None, 3) is None

hints: Search for the node, assigning recursive results back.
With at most one child, return that child.
With two, copy the right subtree's minimum and delete it there.
lessons.explanation: Copy the successor's value into the node, then delete that successor from the right subtree. The successor has no left child, so the second deletion is always one of the easy cases.

lessons.title: Keep a min-heap in a plain list
lessons.body:
# Keep a min-heap in a plain list

A heap is a tree stored in a list: the children of index i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and every parent is no larger than its children. The smallest item is always at index 0.

```python
heap = [1, 4, 2, 9]
i = 3
print((i - 1) // 2)   # parent index 1
```

## Think before coding

Push appends and sifts the new item up while it is smaller than its parent. Pop moves the last item to the root and sifts it down, swapping with the smaller child. Both take about log2(n) swaps. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write push(heap, value) and pop(heap) for a min-heap kept in a list, without the heapq module. pop removes and returns the smallest item.

checks.name: sorted output
heap property
duplicates and single
random

hints: Parent of i is (i - 1) // 2.
Sift up after push while the parent is larger.
After moving the last item to the root, swap with the smaller child.
lessons.explanation: Push appends and sifts the new item up while it is smaller than its parent. Pop moves the last item to the root and sifts it down, swapping with the smaller child. Both take about log2(n) swaps.

lessons.title: Pick the k smallest with heapq
lessons.body:
# Pick the k smallest with heapq

Python's heapq module implements the heap from the previous lesson on plain lists. heapify arranges a list in linear time, and heappop returns the smallest item in logarithmic time.

```python
import heapq
scores = [42, 7, 19, 3]
heapq.heapify(scores)
print(heapq.heappop(scores))   # 3
```

## Think before coding

Sorting everything costs n log n even when you need three items. Popping k times from a heap costs n plus k log n. Copy the input first, because heapify rearranges the list it is given. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write k_smallest(items, k) returning the k smallest values in ascending order using heapq, without modifying items. If k exceeds the length, return all values sorted.
lessons.solution:
import heapq

def k_smallest(items, k):
    heap = list(items)
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    return [heapq.heappop(heap) for _ in range(min(k, len(heap)))]
hints: Copy the list.
heapq.heapify the copy.
heappop min(k, len) times.
lessons.explanation: Sorting everything costs n log n even when you need three items. Popping k times from a heap costs n plus k log n. Copy the input first, because heapify rearranges the list it is given.

lessons.title: Store words letter by letter in a trie
lessons.body:
# Store words letter by letter in a trie

A trie is a tree of nested dictionaries, one letter per level. Words that share a prefix share the path for it, so finding every word that starts with "ca" means walking two steps and collecting what lies below.

```python
root = {}
node = root
for letter in "cat":
    node = node.setdefault(letter, {})
node["$"] = True   # a word ends here
```

## Think before coding

The end marker distinguishes a stored word from a mere prefix: "car" can be a word while "ca" is not. Collect words with a depth-first walk that carries the letters so far, then sort the result for a stable order. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write a Trie class with add(word), contains(word) and complete(prefix). complete returns every stored word starting with prefix, sorted.

prefix is not a word

assert t.contains('car') and not t.contains('ca')

checks.name: no match

assert t.complete('b') == [] and t.complete('') == ['a']

checks.name: empty word
checks.code:
t=Trie(); t.add('')
assert t.contains('') and t.complete('') == ['']

hints: Walk or create one dict per letter.
Mark the end of a word with '$'.
Walk from the prefix node and collect letters until each '$'.
lessons.explanation: The end marker distinguishes a stored word from a mere prefix: "car" can be a word while "ca" is not. Collect words with a depth-first walk that carries the letters so far, then sort the result for a stable order.

lessons.title: Join sets quickly with union-find
lessons.body:
# Join sets quickly with union-find

Union-find tracks which items belong together, such as connected computers or merged accounts. Each item points to a parent; following parents reaches a root that names the whole set.

```python
parent = {x: x for x in "abc"}
parent["b"] = "a"      # b joins a's set
```

## Think before coding

Path compression makes every node on a find path point straight at the root, so later finds are almost instant. Union just points one root at the other. Two items are connected when their roots are equal. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write a UnionFind class built from an iterable of items, with find(x), union(a, b) and connected(a, b). Use path compression in find.

checks.name: joins
checks.code:
u=UnionFind('abcd'); u.union('a','b'); u.union('c','d')
assert u.connected('a','b') and not u.connected('a','c')

checks.name: compression
checks.code:
u=UnionFind(range(4)); u.parent={0:0,1:0,2:1,3:2}
assert u.find(3) == 0 and u.parent[3] == 0 and u.parent[2] == 0

hints: Follow parent links until a node is its own parent.
Point every node on the path at that root.
Union links one root under the other.
lessons.explanation: Path compression makes every node on a find path point straight at the root, so later finds are almost instant. Union just points one root at the other. Two items are connected when their roots are equal.

lessons.title: Evict the least recently used key
lessons.body:
# Evict the least recently used key

A cache keeps a limited number of results. When it is full, a least recently used policy drops the key nobody has touched for the longest time. OrderedDict remembers order and can move a key to the end in constant time.

```python
from collections import OrderedDict
recent = OrderedDict(a=1, b=2)
recent.move_to_end("a")
print(list(recent))   # ['b', 'a']
```

## Think before coding

Treat the end of the dictionary as most recent. Both get and put on an existing key move it there. When an insert exceeds capacity, popitem(last=False) removes the oldest key from the front. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write LRUCache(capacity) with get(key), returning None when missing, and put(key, value). A full cache evicts the least recently used key.

checks.name: evicts oldest
checks.code:
c=LRUCache(2); c.put('a',1); c.put('b',2); c.put('c',3)
assert c.get('a') is None and c.get('c') == 3

checks.name: get refreshes
checks.code:
c=LRUCache(2); c.put('a',1); c.put('b',2); c.get('a'); c.put('c',3)
assert c.get('b') is None and c.get('a') == 1

checks.name: update refreshes
checks.code:
c=LRUCache(2); c.put('a',1); c.put('b',2); c.put('a',9); c.put('c',3)
assert c.get('a') == 9 and c.get('b') is None

hints: Keep the data in an OrderedDict.
move_to_end on every get hit and put.
popitem(last=False) when over capacity.
lessons.explanation: Treat the end of the dictionary as most recent. Both get and put on an existing key move it there. When an insert exceeds capacity, popitem(last=False) removes the oldest key from the front.

lessons.title: Find the fewest steps with breadth-first search
lessons.body:
# Find the fewest steps with breadth-first search

Breadth-first search explores a graph in rings: every node one step away, then every node two steps away. The first time it reaches a node, it has used the fewest possible edges.

```python
graph = {"a": ["b", "c"], "b": ["d"],
         "c": ["d"], "d": []}
# ring 0: a   ring 1: b, c   ring 2: d
```

## Think before coding

Use a deque as the queue and mark nodes when they are added, not when they are taken out, so nothing is queued twice. Store each node's parent to rebuild the path backwards from the goal. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write shortest_path(graph, start, goal) for an adjacency dict. Return the list of nodes on a path with the fewest edges, or None when goal cannot be reached. Visit neighbours in listed order.
lessons.starter:
def shortest_path(graph, start, goal):
    return [start, goal]
hints: Queue the start and record its parent as None.
Record a parent when you first see a neighbour.
Walk parents back from the goal and reverse.
lessons.explanation: Use a deque as the queue and mark nodes when they are added, not when they are taken out, so nothing is queued twice. Store each node's parent to rebuild the path backwards from the goal.

lessons.title: Count connected groups with depth-first search
lessons.body:
# Count connected groups with depth-first search

Depth-first search follows one path as far as it goes before backing up. Started from every unvisited node, it splits an undirected graph into connected components, such as friend circles or separate road networks.

```python
stack = ["a"]
seen = {"a"}
node = stack.pop()
# push a's unseen neighbours next
```

## Think before coding

An explicit stack avoids Python's recursion limit on long chains. Every node is pushed at most once because it is marked when pushed, so the whole count is linear in nodes plus edges. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write count_components(graph) for an undirected adjacency dict (every edge listed both ways). Return the number of connected components.

checks.name: long chain

hints: Loop over every node as a possible start.
Each unseen start begins a new component.
Use a stack to mark everything reachable from it.
lessons.explanation: An explicit stack avoids Python's recursion limit on long chains. Every node is pushed at most once because it is marked when pushed, so the whole count is linear in nodes plus edges.

lessons.title: Find cheapest routes with Dijkstra's algorithm
lessons.body:
# Find cheapest routes with Dijkstra's algorithm

When edges have costs, the fewest edges is not the cheapest route. Dijkstra's algorithm always settles the closest unsettled node next, using a heap of tentative distances.

```python
import heapq
frontier = [(0, "a")]
cost, node = heapq.heappop(frontier)
```

## Think before coding

With non-negative costs, the cheapest entry in the heap can never be improved later, so it is final. Skip stale heap entries whose cost is larger than the best known distance instead of deleting them. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write distances(graph, start) where graph maps a node to a list of (neighbour, cost) pairs with non-negative costs. Return a dict of the cheapest cost to every reachable node.

checks.name: grid

hints: Start with best = {start: 0} and a heap of (0, start).
Skip popped entries worse than best[node].
Push a neighbour whenever its cost improves.
lessons.explanation: With non-negative costs, the cheapest entry in the heap can never be improved later, so it is final. Skip stale heap entries whose cost is larger than the best known distance instead of deleting them.

lessons.title: Count islands on a grid
lessons.body:
# Count islands on a grid

A grid is a graph in disguise: each cell is a node and its up, down, left and right neighbours are edges. Counting islands of land is counting connected components of land cells.

```python
grid = ["LL.",
        ".L.",
        "..L"]
# two islands: diagonal cells do not touch
```

## Think before coding

Scan every cell. When an unvisited land cell appears, count a new island and flood from it, marking every land cell you can reach. Check the bounds before indexing so the edges of the grid are safe. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write count_islands(grid), where grid is a list of equal-length strings with "L" for land and "." for water. Neighbours touch up, down, left or right.
lessons.starter:
def count_islands(grid):
    return sum(row.count('L') for row in grid)
hints: Visit every cell once in a double loop.
Each new unvisited L starts an island.
Flood with a stack over the four neighbours inside the grid.
lessons.explanation: Scan every cell. When an unvisited land cell appears, count a new island and flood from it, marking every land cell you can reach. Check the bounds before indexing so the edges of the grid are safe.

lessons.title: Handle negative costs with Bellman-Ford
lessons.body:
# Handle negative costs with Bellman-Ford

Dijkstra's algorithm breaks when an edge can lower a cost after a node is settled. Bellman-Ford instead relaxes every edge again and again. A shortest path uses at most n - 1 edges, so n - 1 rounds are enough.

```python
edges = [("a", "b", 4), ("a", "c", 2),
         ("c", "b", -3)]
# a -> c -> b costs -1, cheaper than a -> b
```

## Think before coding

If any edge still improves a distance after n - 1 rounds, a cycle with negative total cost is reachable and no cheapest path exists. Report that instead of returning wrong numbers. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write bellman_ford(nodes, edges, start) with edges as (u, v, cost). Return a dict of cheapest costs to reachable nodes, or None when a negative cycle is reachable from start.

checks.name: chain
checks.code:
n=list(range(6)); e=[(i,i+1,-1) for i in range(5)]
assert bellman_ford(n,e,0)[5] == -5

hints: Repeat len(nodes) - 1 rounds of relaxing every edge.
Only relax from nodes that already have a cost.
One more improving edge afterwards means a negative cycle.
lessons.explanation: If any edge still improves a distance after n - 1 rounds, a cycle with negative total cost is reachable and no cheapest path exists. Report that instead of returning wrong numbers.

lessons.title: Remember answers with memoization
lessons.task: Write climb_ways(n) returning the number of ways to climb n stairs with steps of 1 or 2. climb_ways(0) is 1. It must handle n = 5000 quickly.
hints: ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2).
Keep only the last two answers.
Loop upward instead of recursing.
lessons.explanation: The last step was either one stair or two, so ways(n) = ways(n - 1) + ways(n - 2). A table filled from the bottom gives the same numbers without recursion and works for very large n.

lessons.title: Fill a table for the fewest coins
lessons.body:
# Fill a table for the fewest coins

Greedy change fails for coins 1, 3 and 4 with amount 6: taking 4 first needs three coins, while 3 + 3 needs two. Dynamic programming tries every last coin for every smaller amount.

```python
coins = [1, 3, 4]
# fewest coins for amounts 0..4
best = [0, 1, 2, 1, 1]
```

## Think before coding

best[a] is one plus the smallest best[a - coin] over coins that fit. Fill amounts from zero upward so every smaller answer is ready. Amounts no combination reaches stay infinite and become -1. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write fewest_coins(coins, amount) returning the minimum number of coins summing to amount, with unlimited coins of each value, or -1 if impossible.
hints: best[0] is 0 and everything else starts infinite.
For each amount try every coin that fits.
Return -1 if the final entry is still infinite.
lessons.explanation: best[a] is one plus the smallest best[a - coin] over coins that fit. Fill amounts from zero upward so every smaller answer is ready. Amounts no combination reaches stay infinite and become -1.

lessons.title: Compare two strings with a 2D table
lessons.body:
# Compare two strings with a 2D table

A subsequence keeps characters in order but may skip some. The longest common subsequence of two texts measures how similar they are, and diff tools build on the same table.

```python
a, b = "abcde", "ace"
# common subsequence: "ace", length 3
```

## Think before coding

Cell (i, j) holds the answer for the first i characters of a and the first j of b. Equal last characters extend the diagonal answer by one; otherwise take the better of dropping a character from either text. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write lcs_length(a, b) returning the length of the longest common subsequence of two strings.
lessons.starter:
def lcs_length(a, b):
    return len(set(a) & set(b))
hints: Make a (len(a)+1) by (len(b)+1) table of zeros.
Matching characters add one to the diagonal cell.
Otherwise copy the larger of the cell above and to the left.
lessons.explanation: Cell (i, j) holds the answer for the first i characters of a and the first j of b. Equal last characters extend the diagonal answer by one; otherwise take the better of dropping a character from either text.

lessons.title: Backtrack through N queens
lessons.body:
# Backtrack through N queens

Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time and undoes a choice as soon as it cannot lead anywhere. For N queens, place one queen per row and reject any column or diagonal already under attack.

```python
cols, diag1, diag2 = set(), set(), set()
row, col = 2, 1
print(row - col, row + col)   # 1 3
```

## Think before coding

Cells on one diagonal share row - col; cells on the other share row + col. Three sets make each safety check constant time. After exploring a placement, remove it from the sets so the next column starts clean. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write solve(n) returning every solution as a list of column indices, one per row, in lexicographic order.

checks.name: valid
checks.code:
for s in solve(6):
    assert len(set(s)) == 6 and len({r-c for r,c in enumerate(s)}) == 6 and len({r+c for r,c in enumerate(s)}) == 6

hints: Place one queen per row, trying columns left to right.
Track used columns and both diagonals in sets.
Undo the placement after the recursive call.
lessons.explanation: Cells on one diagonal share row - col; cells on the other share row + col. Three sets make each safety check constant time. After exploring a placement, remove it from the sets so the next column starts clean.

lessons.title: Never step back with Knuth-Morris-Pratt
lessons.body:
# Never step back with Knuth-Morris-Pratt

Naive matching restarts after every mismatch and can compare the same text characters many times. Knuth-Morris-Pratt first studies the pattern: for each prefix it records the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.

```python
pattern = "abab"
failure = [0, 0, 1, 2]
# after a full "abab" match,
# "ab" counts toward the next one
```

## Think before coding

On a mismatch, fall back through the failure table instead of moving backwards in the text. Each text character is read once, so the search is linear in text plus pattern, and overlapping matches are found naturally. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write find_all(text, pattern) returning every start index of pattern in text, overlaps included, in linear time. A non-empty pattern is guaranteed.
hints: Build failure[i]: longest proper prefix of pattern[:i+1] that is also its suffix.
On mismatch set k = failure[k - 1] instead of moving back.
After a full match record it and continue from failure[k - 1].
lessons.explanation: On a mismatch, fall back through the failure table instead of moving backwards in the text. Each text character is read once, so the search is linear in text plus pattern, and overlapping matches are found naturally.

lessons.title: Order tasks with depth-first topological sort
lessons.body:
# Order tasks with depth-first topological sort

Build steps, course prerequisites and spreadsheet formulas form directed graphs without cycles. A topological order lists every task after everything it depends on.

```python
needs = {"test": ["build"],
         "build": ["fetch"], "fetch": []}
# fetch, build, test
```

## Think before coding

Depth-first search can emit a node after all of its dependencies have been emitted. Three states detect cycles: unvisited, in progress and done. Meeting a node that is still in progress means a cycle, so no order exists. Work through the example by hand before changing the starter. Decide what should happen for an empty input, a single value and a repeated value where those cases apply. The checks use several inputs so a hard-coded answer cannot stand in for the rule.
lessons.task: Write build_order(needs) where needs maps each task to the tasks it depends on. Return a list with dependencies first, visiting tasks and dependencies in the given order, or raise ValueError on a cycle.

checks.name: cycle

hints: Track each task as active or done.
Visit every dependency before appending the task.
Seeing an active task again means a cycle.
lessons.explanation: Depth-first search can emit a node after all of its dependencies have been emitted. Three states detect cycles: unvisited, in progress and done. Meeting a node that is still in progress means a cycle, so no order exists.
